(News 10) - A bat in Livingston County has tested positive for rabies, the first reported animal case in the county this year, according to the Livingston County Health Department. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention say 75% of Americans live in an area where animals carry rabies, and contact with infected bats is the leading cause of human rabies deaths in the United States. The Livingston County Health Department says a bat can expose a person to rabies even without a visible bite or scratch. Contact with a bat’s saliva or brain tissue, or even finding a bat in a room upon waking up, could be enough to warrant getting tested. What to do if bitten or scratched Health officials are reminding residents to take precautions if they encounter a bat. Anyone who is bitten or scratched should immediately wash the affected area with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to local health officials. Bat removal calls average 10 to 20 a day Ash Bigger, owner of Bat and Wildlife Solutions, helps dozens of families remove bats from their homes every day. “We usually average about anywhere from 10 to 20 a day with bats in the home, hearing scratching, things like that,” said Ash Bigger, owner-operator, Bat and Wildlife Solutions. Bigger says if a bat is found in a home, plan the next move carefully. “You want to try to keep an eye on the bat or corral it into a bedroom, bathroom to confine it into a certain space. If it’s loose in the house, these things hide so well, it’s virtually impossible to find them if you lose sight of them,” Bigger said. “You definitely want to protect yourself if you were to try to capture the bat and get it tested. You want to wear thick leather gloves, try to wrap it up in a towel. You definitely don’t want to try to grab it barehanded,” Bigger said. Sealing gaps can keep bats out Bigger says bats are opportunists. To keep them out of a home, he recommends sealing up any gaps around the roof line, since bats can fit through holes as small as a dime. The health department also recommends taking steps to prevent bats from entering homes, including keeping doors and windows closed and locked and sealing small openings where bats could get inside. Residents who find a bat in their home or have questions about potential rabies exposure should contact their local health department or a health care provider. CHARLOTTE, N.C. (QUEEN CITY NEWS) -- A rapid bat was found near a Ballantyne apartment complex this week, making the eight such case in Mecklenburg County this year. The Charlotte-Mecklenburg Animal Care & Control was notified that a rabies alert was sent out at 7 p.m. Wednesday, Aug. 26. The alert was sent to residents that reside in the 14200 block of Ballantyne Lake Road. A bat in this area tested positive for rabies. There were two human exposures reported, and no domestic pet exposures. Advertisement Advertisement CMS investigation into Superintendent Crystal Hill has cost nearly $380,000: records If you have any questions regarding potential human exposures, contact Communicable Disease at 980-314-9201. Out of the county's eight cases, this was the third involving a bat this year. Two cases were found in raccoons. Five rabid bats were discovered a year ago. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. The Charlotte-Mecklenburg Animal Care & Control issued a rabies alert to residents in the 14200 block of Ballantyne Lake Road. This case is the third bat-related rabies case in Mecklenburg County this year, contributing to a total of eight cases. Two human exposures were reported, with no domestic pet exposures. The alert was sent out at 7 p.m. on the same day, and residents are encouraged to contact Communicable Disease for more information. The incident highlights ongoing rabies activity in the area, with similar cases noted in the past year.

news.content: Latest U.S. Iran War Nepal Flood World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds Philadelphia | News Weather Sports Video CBS Philadelphia Shows 81° All News Pennsylvania New Jersey Delaware National World Health Entertainment Politics Traffic & Transportation Business Recalls Latest Weather Radars Closings & Delays All Sports CBS Sports HQ Eagles Sixers Phillies Flyers Blue Coats College High School Odds Focusing on the Future Gallen of Questions Alex's Lemonade Stand Lights for the Fight More Than Pink Friday Football Frenzy Hispanic Heritage Month Joy of Sharing Black Business Month Mental Reset RMHC Telethon Summer Beat Spreading the Love The Heartbeat Station Info Contact Us Share Photos & Video Send Us a News Tip Advertise With Us Contests & Promotions Download The App About NEXTGEN TV Photo Galleries Mentioned On-Air Jobs & Internships Memorials Watch CBS News Local News Raccoon tests positive for rabies in Camden County, New Jersey, health officials say By Frederick Sutton Sinclair August 27, 2026 / 11:24 AM EDT / CBS Philadelphia Add CBS News on Google A raccoon that was in an altercation with a dog in Gloucester Township, New Jersey, tested positive for rabies, health officials said. On Aug. 22, a Barrington resident's dog got into an altercation with a raccoon in their backyard. Animal control captured the raccoon and arranged for it to be tested for rabies at the state Public Health & Environmental Laboratories in Trenton. The Camden County Health Department was notified Aug. 26 that the raccoon tested positive for rabies. There were no known human exposures to the raccoon. The dog's owner was notified of the positive rabies test. The dog was vaccinated for rabies and received a booster shot. It will remain under confinement and observation for 45 days. "Rabies is a serious illness, but it can be prevented by early treatment after exposure," said Commissioner Jennifer Cooley Fleisher, liaison to the Camden County Department of Health and Human Services. "If you have been bitten or scratched by a wild animal, it is important that you seek immediate medical attention." In a press release, Fleisher listed several steps Camden County residents can take to protect themselves and their pets: Keep vaccinations up to date for all dogs, cats and ferrets. Keep your pets under direct supervision so they do not come in contact with wild animals. If your pet is bitten by a wild animal, seek veterinary assistance for the pet immediately. Contact your local animal control agency to remove any stray animals from your neighborhood. Fleisher also urges residents to avoid direct contact with unfamiliar animals: Enjoy wild animals such as raccoons, skunks and foxes from afar. Do not handle, feed or unintentionally attract wild animals with open garbage cans or litter. Never adopt wild animals or bring them into your home. Do not try to nurse sick animals to health. Call animal control or an animal rescue agency for assistance. Teach children never to handle unfamiliar animals, wild or domestic, even if they seem friendly. Prevent bats from entering living quarters or occupied spaces in homes, churches, schools and other similar areas where they might come in contact with people or pets. When traveling abroad, avoid direct contact with wild animals. Health Doctor shares PSA after waking up to a bat trying to ‘burrow’ into her mouth By Allie Yang Published Aug. 27, 2026, 10:01 a.m. ET 214214 Comments 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE See more of our coverage in your search results. Add The New York Post on Google Dr. Krista Edelman was having a strange dream about a small mouse trying to get into her mouth. When she woke up, she was met with the horrifying realization that there was, in fact, a furry animal “burrowing” between her lips. “I reach up to my mouth ... and then I touch something that is kind of slimy and a little hairy and cool,” she said in an Instagram post, describing a half-awake state when she thought she was still dreaming. She realized “immediately” it was a bat. 4 Dr. Krista Edelman woke up to find a bat trying to get into her mouth. WTVR “This bat was legitimately trying to burrow between my lips into my mouth, trying to get past my teeth,” said Edelman, a gastroenterologist in Richmond, Virginia. “I grabbed this bat and I threw it across the room and I screamed.” Her husband grabbed a T-ball bat to take care of it, but from her training, she says she knew that wasn’t the right move. “I knew we were supposed to try to catch this bat so it can actually be tested and see if there are rabies in its brain,” she said. There are more than 40 bat species across the US, and healthy bats avoid humans if they can help it. But summertime is when homeowners frequently find bats in their home. The mammals often roost in the attic, and if it gets too hot, they’ll leave to find a cooler spot. Bats can infect humans with a number of dangerous diseases. Famously, COVID-19 originated from the mammal. 4 “I reach up to my mouth ... and then I touch something that is kind of slimy and a little hairy and cool,” Edelman said in an Instagram post. Krista Edelman / Instagram Rabies is one of the primary diseases that can be passed from bats to humans. A vast majority (97%) of bats are healthy and good for the environment, but infected bats are responsible for 7 of 10 rabies deaths in the US. Untreated, rabies travels slowly through the body over months without symptoms, then cause serious brain and nervous system damage, leading to coma and death. 4 Edelman was able to trap the bat in a bucket to get it tested. Krista Edelman / Instagram Luckily, the rabies vaccine is very effective and can be given to people shortly after they’ve been exposed. It helps the body kills the virus before it reaches the brain. In Edelman’s case, the bat tested negative for rabies — but she still took action to be on the safe side. “Because I had direct contact and hadn’t previously been vaccinated against rabies, I went to the ER and started the rabies vaccine series and received immunoglobulin,” she said. Most importantly, Edelman wanted to share a PSA: “If you live in an older home, check those attics and chimneys! And if you wake up with a bat in the room and aren’t sure whether you had contact with it, don’t assume you’re fine. It’s worth getting medical advice right away!” 4 Bats are known to carry the rabies virus. Krista Edelman / Instagram Why you may not know if a bat touched you Not everyone who encounters a bat will even know a bat touched them. Bat bites, the primary way rabies is spread, can be very small and not easily seen. Experts recommend proceeding as if there was a known bat bite if a bat was found where people were asleep, or there were children or someone else might not be able to understand or report a bat encounter. Here’s what to do if you suspect a bat touched someone in your house: Never touch the bat with bare hands — that’s one way rabies can spread. Gently capture the bat when it lands in a large box or bucket, while wearing thick leather gloves. Puncture air holes, slide cardboard or another rigid flat surface under the opening, flip it upside down and tape it shut (just like capturing a bug). Call your state health department. They’ll have the bat tested for rabies and will determine if you need medical attention. 214 What do you think? Post a comment. How to keep bats out of your home: Bats don’t make holes — they use existing ones to get in. They can fit into tiny openings, as small as 1/4 inch wide. Check for any openings. Call animal control or a local wildlife conservation to help bat proof your home. Use caulk, screens and steel wool to fill holes and seal doors, especially around the attic. Ensure all windows and doors are closed tightly. SPONSORED STORIES Dr. Krista Edelman woke up to find a bat trying to get into her mouth. (CDC) The Brief A dead bat found in the Terry Mill Road area tested positive for rabies on Friday, health officials said. Georgia is considered a rabies-endemic state, and DeKalb County officials routinely report several cases of the virus each year. Health officials urge residents to keep pet vaccinations up to date, secure trash containers, and remove outdoor feeding stations. DEKALB COUNTY, Ga. - Health officials are warning DeKalb County residents after a dead bat tested positive for rabies. What we know: County officials confirmed a dead bat located along Terry Mill Road tested positive for rabies on Friday. Since Georgia is an endemic state, the virus remains present year-round, making local wildlife cases relatively common. Rabies is a viral disease that attacks the central nervous system and brain. While it primarily spreads between animals, it can transfer to humans through saliva, typically via a bite or scratch. What we don't know: It's unclear if any humans or domestic pets came into contact with, were bitten by, or were scratched by the infected bat. What you can do: Officials emphasize that rabies vaccinations are highly effective at protecting both humans and domestic pets. Under county rules, residents are required to vaccinate their pets annually and register their rabies tags with local authorities. County officials advise residents to eliminate outdoor pet feeding stations and ensure garbage cans are tightly sealed to avoid attracting wild animals. Authorities also urge owners to monitor their pets for any unusual behavior, noting that DeKalb County Animal Control will only set wild animal traps if a person or domestic pet has been bitten or scratched. Officials emphasize that anyone bitten or scratched by a wild or unknown animal should seek immediate medical treatment. To report an animal bite or request information, residents can call DeKalb County Animal Control during standard business hours Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., at 404-294-2996 (extension 2), or reach their after-hours emergency line at 404-294-2519. The Source: The information in this story came from a news release from DeKalb County Government. news.source_body_en: A dead bat found along Terry Mill Road in DeKalb County, Georgia, tested positive for rabies on Friday, August 21, 2026, according to DeKalb County officials. The report was published on August 25, 2026. Rabies is a fatal but preventable viral disease that attacks the central nervous system and brain. It primarily spreads between animals but can be transmitted to humans through saliva, typically via a bite or scratch. While the bat's rabies status is confirmed, it is unclear if any humans or domestic pets were exposed. Health officials are advising residents to ensure their pets are vaccinated and to secure trash and outdoor feeding stations to prevent attracting wild animals. They also recommend monitoring pets for unusual behavior and contacting DeKalb County Animal Control if a person or domestic pet has been bitten or scratched. The incident highlights the ongoing presence of rabies in Georgia, an endemic state, and the importance of preventive measures.

news.content: Issues Actions Petitions Pledges Timeline Politics Justice Environment Health Culture War Latest Originals Donate Sign Up Search Saturday, August 29, 2026 NationofChange Issues Actions Petitions Pledges Timeline Politics Justice Environment Health Culture War Latest Originals Donate Sign Up Environment A deadly cross over: In South Africa, rabies moves from land animals to seals Cases have been confirmed along the Western Cape and Northern Cape coastlines since May 2024. A South African government agency says it is the first time rabies has established itself in a marine mammal population anywhere in the world. By Andy Lehren - August 24, 2026 57 SOURCEMongabay Share on Facebook Tweet on Twitter tweet Cape fur seals at a breeding colony. Photo: Hans Hillewaert / CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Cape Town, South Africa, has recorded 135 incidents of aggressive seal behavior toward humans since September 2021, including injuries that led to hospitalizations. Researchers suspect the cause is rabies, a disease normally associated with land animals but has leapt to Cape fur seals. Since May 2024, rabies cases have been confirmed in Cape fur seals along the Western Cape and Northern Cape coastlines of South Africa — the first time the virus has established itself in a marine mammal population anywhere in the world. Beyond attacks on humans, researchers worry whether the disease will spread to other marine mammals, as seals interact with different species. CAPE TOWN, South Africa — Debbie Hendrikz was walking along her usual route on the shoreline when she crouched to photograph a seal. She is familiar with seals and has captured similar images along the beach. But this was different. “It just went for me,” the 49-year-old said. “I knew instinctively by the sound it made that I was its prey. It grabbed my arm and bit hard into a metal bracelet I was wearing, which saved me. I knew I had to get away and not let it get my feet in the soft sand. I managed to shake it off my arm and just got away.” “I never imagined anything like this could happen. It took me a long while to get over it.” Seals do not normally see humans as prey, but Hendrikz’s encounter is one of a growing list of recent attacks by the marine mammals in Cape Town. According to Gregg Oelofse, the City of Cape Town’s coastal manager, the city has recorded 135 incidents of aggressive seal behavior toward humans since September 2021. More than half, 73 incidents, resulted in bite injuries ranging from broken skin to those requiring hospitalization in an intensive care unit. Researchers in South Africa suspect the incidents stem from a disease normally associated with land animals that appears to be leaping to Cape fur seals (Arctocephalus pusillus) — rabies. According to South Africa’s National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD), reports of rabies in seals around the world prior to 2024 were exceedingly rare. But since May 2024, multiple cases have been confirmed in Cape fur seals along the Western Cape and Northern Cape coastlines of South Africa. The government agency said it believes it is the first time rabies has established and maintained itself in a marine mammal population anywhere in the world. Now South African government officials and researchers are examining how seals contracted the disease in the first place. They are taking steps to stop the spread of rabies, but say they are also worried that, as seals travel great distances and interact with other species, the virus could jump to other marine mammals and perhaps even bring rabies to Antarctica, where it has never been. ‘No longer eradicable’ Experts at a July 2025 scientific workshop in Cape Town attended by Mongabay concluded that the disease is now likely endemic in Cape fur seals and is no longer eradicable. They categorized it as a persistent threat requiring long-term management. Scientists are now asking deeper questions about whether this outbreak is slowly burning itself out or if the cases are a prelude to something far larger, with rabies spreading to other sea mammals. To date, the NICD says rabies has not been found in any other marine mammal species along South Africa’s coast. South African scientists say they believe the rabies in seals started on land. According to a July 2024 outbreak update report by South Africa’s Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development (DALRRD), genetic sequencing of the virus found in infected seals points to a canid origin, most closely linked to a rabies strain from black-backed jackals (Lupulella mesomelas) from Namibia. The DALRRD report came the same month as a Cape Town workshop with a wide range of participants, including leading scientists from different countries. DALRRD’s working hypothesis, developed further in an updated report published in October 2024, is that a rabid jackal bit a seal somewhere on the Namibian coast — a plausible scenario given that jackals are known to prey on seal pups there, biting seals and getting into skirmishes with adults protecting their young. DALRRD also reported there may be more than one event that introduced rabies into the seal population, including a secondary link to a strain of rabies from a bat-eared fox (Otocyon megalotis) from South Africa’s Western Cape. What happened next was then perhaps inevitable. Cape fur seals are social animals living in enormous, densely packed colonies. Physical contact, including biting, is constant. In the terminal stages of rabies infection, the virus drives animals to bite. In a colony of thousands of seals in close confines on an island or outcrop these factors would create a near perfect transmission environment. According to the DALRRD October 2024 report, genetic sequencing of multiple samples showed sequences clustering together, indicating the virus was already circulating within the seal population and representing what scientists now describe as a canid rabies Cape fur seal cycle. The NICD’s August 2025 briefing document records that between May 2024 and January 2025, a total of 39 cases were confirmed from the Western Cape and a further 16 from the Northern Cape province. In June 2025, the first case was confirmed in the Eastern Cape. Critically, DALRRD’s October 2024 report also documents that the outbreak is not new: Retrospective testing of stored samples from Cape fur seal deaths dating back to 2021 returned some positive results, indicating the virus has been present longer. Coastal manager Gregg Oelofse’s statistics from the field suggest a more specific timeline. The city first recorded a marked change in seal aggression in September 2021, beginning with an incident at Miller’s Point in the Western Cape. In the previous two decades, his team logged only two comparable cases. Within months of September 2021, however, reports of aggressive seals were coming in from across the peninsula, Oelofse said. Surfers showed photographs of bitten surfboards, swimmers recalled being chased from the water. At the time, rabies was not considered, since the disease had never before been recorded in a marine mammal. The working theory that first emerged was domoic acid poisoning from harmful algal blooms. That theory did not hold up. The earliest confirmed positive case of rabies came from retrospective testing of a brain sample taken from a seal removed from Kommetjie, in the Western Cape, after it had bitten an elderly woman walking on the beach in early July 2022. The seal died en route to the Cape of Good Hope’s Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. At the time, no one suspected rabies, Oelofse said. It was only in April 2024, when four seals were tested and three came back positive, that the city and its scientific partners recognized rabies was established in the population. Retrospective testing of stored samples, including the 2022 Kommetjie case, confirming the earlier presence of the disease and its link with aggressive attacks. Will rabies spread further in seals? Now researchers are trying to better understand how the disease in Cape fur seals will spread. To understand where this is going, science needs a number. Specifically, it needs what epidemiologists call the basic reproductive number, R, the average number of new infections generated by a single infected individual in a susceptible population. The logic is if the R number falls below one, then each infected animal generates less than one new case on average. The chain of transmission then weakens, and the disease eventually burns out. But if the number is above one, each infection spawns more than one new case and the epidemic grows. Johann Kotze, a freelance veterinarian and epidemiologist who presented his modelling findings at the July 2025 Cape Town workshop, has been constructing an epidemiological model specifically for this outbreak. His preliminary results offer the first quantitative foothold on the question. The spread observed so far is slow, he said, rather than an explosively growing outbreak. This is consistent with a very low R number, Kotze said: “Only a very low R number would produce what we are seeing. Higher values would have grown much quicker, much faster.” His current estimate puts the R number below 1.1 and possibly below 1.05. For further context, an R number of 1.05 means that on average, every 100 infected seals would generate 105 new cases. The current estimate is above one, which means the virus is sustaining itself and slowly expanding. Experts at the July 2025 workshop put it plainly: Unlike the rapid, large-scale die-offs seen with other diseases, rabies may burn slowly through populations, flaring unpredictably. It is a slow burn, not an explosion. The question for scientists, then, is whether the pattern remains this way. On the ground in Cape Town, according to Oelofse, the pattern appears to be holding. “It’s kind of like it goes dead quiet for a while and then suddenly we’ll have three rabid seals in Kommetjie that came from Duiker Island,” he said. “And then it’ll go quiet for a while and then we’ll suddenly have one or two in Simon’s Town that came from Seal Island.” On another occasion, his colleague was called out to Big Bay twice in a single day for two separate rabid seals, he added. The pattern matches what scientists predicted at the outset: Small flare-ups, clusters of disease positive animals in one location, then nothing; and then a flare-up elsewhere. Researchers still have a lot more to learn about the disease. To refine estimates further, scientific models need answers to difficult questions: How long does an infected seal remain contagious? What is the incubation period? What is the natural turnover rate of the seal population, which incorporates not only their lifespan but also how often new pups are born? How do these factors interact with the virus’s transmission rates? With marine mammals that live across hundreds of kilometer of remote coastline, gathering that data is difficult. The DALRRD October 2024 report recognizes this challenge. Vast stretches of the Northern Cape coastline are sparsely populated and some areas are restricted due to mining activities, so collecting data in those areas is constrained, it said. Oelofse said Cape Town itself has no reliable measure of how many seals are infected at any given time across remote stretches of coastline such as Elands Bay, where seals are plentiful but monitoring is minimal. “We don’t really have a good idea of how present rabies is in the seal population,” he said. “It doesn’t appear to be rampant, but we don’t really know.” Kotze’s modelling so far points to two divergent future paths — rabies fades, or it increases. On the first path, the outbreak may dissipate because the virus encounters barriers like geographical gaps between colonies that limit its spread. The outbreak plateaus and the disease does not become entrenched permanently and gradually fades. This would mirror what happens with other viruses that enter a new host species but ultimately fail to sustain themselves. But the fear is that the current situation will follow the second scenario and that this is the cusp of something larger. On this second path, the disease has a slow beginning. The current case counts could suggest not a plateau but a prologue. Given enough time and enough seals across colonies stretching from the Western Cape to Angola, the virus will spread. Even worse in this scenario, seals then infect other marine mammals and the disease spreads to other species. The difference between these two futures turns largely on how Cape fur seals reproduce. Seals reproduce slowly. This may ultimately limit the virus’s ability to sustain itself; or it means the seal population cannot recover quickly if rabies infections do expand significantly. “The only thing that stops an epidemic of this kind is when you reach a point where the number of new infections equals the number of new births in the population, what we call an endemic state,” Kotze said. The past and the future for rabies and South Africa’s fur seals Cape fur seals have likely become more vulnerable to rabies and other diseases because of ecological pressures. Mass seal deaths in 2021 and 2022, in which thousands of seals died along South Africa’s West Coast, were investigated and attributed primarily to malnutrition. Scientists have pointed to chronically stressed animals living in warming oceans. Available prey has become less reliable. Coastal real estate development has added stress, limiting some of the territory they prefer for their colonies. Harmful algal blooms or red tides happen more often and are larger, affecting seal behavior and cognition. The aggressive encounters that alarmed beachgoers from 2021 onwards were initially attributed to these blooms. Researchers also point to another detail that may point to where the disease is heading: When the seal attacked Debbie Hendrikz on Fish Hoek beach, she did not contract rabies, unlike when a diseased dog bites a person. The NICD notes that to date, there are no known cases where seals transmitted the disease to people. Oelofse, who has tracked the toll of seal attacks on humans closely, called this the most interesting open question in the entire outbreak: Why has rabies not spread from infected seals to the humans they have bitten? His team has gone back and retrospectively contacted people known to have been bitten by confirmed rabid seals — none have developed rabies. Tour guides operating in the area around Duiker Island reported being bitten repeatedly by seals behaving strangely and were not treated for rabies. None became infected. “I think it might be related to the high salt content in the seal’s mouth,” Oelofse said. “It might be diluting the virus. We know salt water has a bit of an antiseptic effect. I don’t know.” Kotze cautioned against speculating on this question, “There is no proof as to why those bites would not have infected the human.” The leading theories involve reduced viral load in the saliva of marine-exposed animals, salt water degrading the virus, and the immediate wound-washing that ocean immersion provides. These theories remain unproven, he said. For now, government officials are cautious. The NICD strongly advises anyone bitten, scratched or licked by a seal suspected of having rabies to wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water and seek immediate treatment at the nearest clinic or hospital. Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis is effective in preventing infection if applied urgently and appropriately. The NICD further advises that those at frequent or continual risk of exposure, such as swimmers, divers, surfers or people working with seals, should discuss pre-exposure prophylaxis with their healthcare provider. The government has considered other efforts to limit the spread of the disease in seals. Mass vaccination of the entire seal population — an approach that has helped control rabies in European foxes — was assessed and declared not feasible by the National Department of Agriculture in its October 2024 report. A key factor cited for the decision is that seal colonies are often inaccessible. But the July 2025 workshop produced a more targeted recommendation: Vaccination trials should begin for seals that frequently interact with humans. The effectiveness of rabies vaccines in marine mammals remains unproven, but experts concluded that the trials pose minimal risk and may prove to provide protection. In August 2024, the world’s first ever rabies vaccination trial in marine mammals took place at Kalk Bay harbor in Cape Town, conducted by the Two Oceans Aquarium Foundation in collaboration with scientific and government partners. The city has since stepped back from continuing to vaccinate the Kalk Bay harbor seal colony. The high turnover of individual seals moving between that colony and Seal Island, approximately 12 km (7.6 mi) east, makes sustained coverage difficult to achieve. A renewed, smaller effort at Gordon’s Bay harbor is being considered, Oelofse said. Authorities have started and continue to vaccinate Southern elephant seals (Mirounga leonina) on the Cape coast. Even though they are a different species and the virus has not been identified in them, officials fear they may contract the disease from fights with Cape fur seals. The concern driving this effort is that elephant seals can travel far: One tagged elephant seal vaccinated in Cape Town later turned up on Marion Island, deep in the Southern Ocean, demonstrating how far and fast the disease could travel if it took hold in a more mobile, far-ranging species. Between 15 and 20 elephant seals have been tagged and vaccinated to date, with booster shots given when possible. There is another seal species that encounters Cape fur seals that has not been vaccinated: sub-Antarctic fur seals (Arctocephalus tropicali). Beyond attacks on humans, researchers worry whether the disease will spread to other marine mammals, as seals interact with different species. CAPE TOWN, South Africa — Debbie Hendrikz was walking along her usual route on the shoreline when she crouched to photograph a seal. She is familiar with seals and has captured similar images along the beach. But this was different. “It just went for me,” the 49-year-old said. “I knew instinctively by the sound it made that I was its prey. It grabbed my arm and bit hard into a metal bracelet I was wearing, which saved me. I knew I had to get away and not let it get my feet in the soft sand. I managed to shake it off my arm and just got away.” “I never imagined anything like this could happen. It took me a long while to get over it.” Seals do not normally see humans as prey, but Hendrikz’s encounter is one of a growing list of recent attacks by the marine mammals in Cape Town. According to Gregg Oelofse, the City of Cape Town’s coastal manager, the city has recorded 135 incidents of aggressive seal behavior toward humans since September 2021. More than half, 73 incidents, resulted in bite injuries ranging from broken skin to those requiring hospitalization in an intensive care unit. Researchers in South Africa suspect the incidents stem from a disease normally associated with land animals that appears to be leaping to Cape fur seals (Arctocephalus pusillus) — rabies. According to South Africa’s National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD), reports of rabies in seals around the world prior to 2024 were exceedingly rare. But since May 2024, multiple cases have been confirmed in Cape fur seals along the Western Cape and Northern Cape coastlines of South Africa. The government agency said it believes it is the first time rabies has established and maintained itself in a marine mammal population anywhere in the world. Now South African government officials and researchers are examining how seals contracted the disease in the first place. They are taking steps to stop the spread of rabies, but say they are also worried that, as seals travel great distances and interact with other species, the virus could jump to other marine mammals and perhaps even bring rabies to Antarctica, where it has never been. ‘No longer eradicable’ Experts at a July 2025 scientific workshop in Cape Town attended by Mongabay concluded that the disease is now likely endemic in Cape fur seals and is no longer eradicable. They categorized it as a persistent threat requiring long-term management. Scientists are now asking deeper questions about whether this outbreak is slowly burning itself out or if the cases are a prelude to something far larger, with rabies spreading to other sea mammals. To date, the NICD says rabies has not been found in any other marine mammal species along South Africa’s coast. South African scientists say they believe the rabies in seals started on land. According to a July 2024 outbreak update report by South Africa’s Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development (DALRRD), genetic sequencing of the virus found in infected seals points to a canid origin, most closely linked to a rabies strain from black-backed jackals (Lupulella mesomelas) from Namibia. The DALRRD report came the same month as a Cape Town workshop with a wide range of participants, including leading scientists from different countries. DALRRD’s working hypothesis, developed further in an updated report published in October 2024, is that a rabid jackal bit a seal somewhere on the Namibian coast — a plausible scenario given that jackals are known to prey on seal pups there, biting seals and getting into skirmishes with adults protecting their young. DALRRD also reported there may be more than one event that introduced rabies into the seal population, including a secondary link to a strain of rabies from a bat-eared fox (Otocyon megalotis) from South Africa’s Western Cape. What happened next was then perhaps inevitable. Cape fur seals are social animals living in enormous, densely packed colonies. Physical contact, including biting, is constant. In the terminal stages of rabies infection, the virus drives animals to bite. In a colony of thousands of seals in close confines on an island or outcrop these factors would create a near perfect transmission environment. According to the DALRRD October 2024 report, genetic sequencing of multiple samples showed sequences clustering together, indicating the virus was already circulating within the seal population and representing what scientists now describe as a canid rabies Cape fur seal cycle. The NICD’s August 2025 briefing document records that between May 2024 and January 2025, a total of 39 cases were confirmed from the Western Cape and a further 16 from the Northern Cape province. In June 2025, the first case was confirmed in the Eastern Cape. Critically, DALRRD’s October 2024 report also documents that the outbreak is not new: Retrospective testing of stored samples from Cape fur seal deaths dating back to 2021 returned some positive results, indicating the virus has been present longer. Coastal manager Gregg Oelofse’s statistics from the field suggest a more specific timeline. The city first recorded a marked change in seal aggression in September 2021, beginning with an incident at Miller’s Point in the Western Cape. In the previous two decades, his team logged only two comparable cases. Within months of September 2021, however, reports of aggressive seals were coming in from across the peninsula, Oelofse said. Surfers showed photographs of bitten surfboards, swimmers recalled being chased from the water. At the time, rabies was not considered, since the disease had never before been recorded in a marine mammal. The working theory that first emerged was domoic acid poisoning from harmful algal blooms. That theory did not hold up. The earliest confirmed positive case of rabies came from retrospective testing of a brain sample taken from a seal removed from Kommetjie, in the Western Cape, after it had bitten an elderly woman walking on the beach in early July 2022. The seal died en route to the Cape of Good Hope’s Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. At the time, no one suspected rabies, Oelofse said. It was only in April 2024, when four seals were tested and three came back positive, that the city and its scientific partners recognized rabies was established in the population. Retrospective testing of stored samples, including the 2022 Kommetjie case, confirming the earlier presence of the disease and its link with aggressive attacks. Will rabies spread further in seals? Now researchers are trying to better understand how the disease in Cape fur seals will spread. To understand where this is going, science needs a number. Specifically, it needs what epidemiologists call the basic reproductive number, R, the average number of new infections generated by a single infected individual in a susceptible population. The logic is if the R number falls below one, then each infected animal generates less than one new case on average. The chain of transmission then weakens, and the disease eventually burns out. But if the number is above one, each infection spawns more than one new case and the epidemic grows. Johann Kotze, a freelance veterinarian and epidemiologist who presented his modelling findings at the July 2025 Cape Town workshop, has been constructing an epidemiological model specifically for this outbreak. His preliminary results offer the first quantitative foothold on the question. The spread observed so far is slow, he said, rather than an explosively growing outbreak. This is consistent with a very low R number, Kotze said: “Only a very low R number would produce what we are seeing. Higher values would have grown much quicker, much faster.” His current estimate puts the R number below 1.1 and possibly below 1.05. For further context, an R number of 1.05 means that on average, every 100 infected seals would generate 105 new cases. The current estimate is above one, which means the virus is sustaining itself and slowly expanding. Experts at the July 2025 workshop put it plainly: Unlike the rapid, large-scale die-offs seen with other diseases, rabies may burn slowly through populations, flaring unpredictably. It is a slow burn, not an explosion. The question for scientists, then, is whether the pattern remains this way. On the ground in Cape Town, according to Oelofse, the pattern appears to be holding. “It’s kind of like it goes dead quiet for a while and then suddenly we’ll have three rabid seals in Kommetjie that came from Duiker Island,” he said. “And then it’ll go quiet for a while and then we’ll suddenly have one or two in Simon’s Town that came from Seal Island.” On another occasion, his colleague was called out to Big Bay twice in a single day for two separate rabid seals, he added. The pattern matches what scientists predicted at the outset: Small flare-ups, clusters of disease positive animals in one location, then nothing; and then a flare-up elsewhere. Researchers still have a lot more to learn about the disease. To refine estimates further, scientific models need answers to difficult questions: How long does an infected seal remain contagious? What is the incubation period? What is the natural turnover rate of the seal population, which incorporates not only their lifespan but also how often new pups are born? How do these factors interact with the virus’s transmission rates? With marine mammals that live across hundreds of kilometer of remote coastline, gathering that data is difficult. The DALRRD October 2024 report recognizes this challenge. Vast stretches of the Northern Cape coastline are sparsely populated and some areas are restricted due to mining activities, so collecting data in those areas is constrained, it said. Oelofse said Cape Town itself has no reliable measure of how many seals are infected at any given time across remote stretches of coastline such as Elands Bay, where seals are plentiful but monitoring is minimal. “We don’t really have a good idea of how present rabies is in the seal population,” he said. “It doesn’t appear to be rampant, but we don’t really know.” Kotze’s modelling so far points to two divergent future paths — rabies fades, or it increases. On the first path, the outbreak may dissipate because the virus encounters barriers like geographical gaps between colonies that limit its spread. The outbreak plateaus and the disease does not become entrenched permanently and gradually fades. This would mirror what happens with other viruses that enter a new host species but ultimately fail to sustain themselves. But the fear is that the current situation will follow the second scenario and that this is the cusp of something larger. On this second path, the disease has a slow beginning. The current case counts could suggest not a plateau but a prologue. Given enough time and enough seals across colonies stretching from the Western Cape to Angola, the virus will spread. Even worse in this scenario, seals then infect other marine mammals and the disease spreads to other species. The difference between these two futures turns largely on how Cape fur seals reproduce. Seals reproduce slowly. This may ultimately limit the virus’s ability to sustain itself; or it means the seal population cannot recover quickly if rabies infections do expand significantly. “The only thing that stops an epidemic of this kind is when you reach a point where the number of new infections equals the number of new births in the population, what we call an endemic state,” Kotze said. The past and the future for rabies and South Africa’s fur seals Cape fur seals have likely become more vulnerable to rabies and other diseases because of ecological pressures. Mass seal deaths in 2021 and 2022, in which thousands of seals died along South Africa’s West Coast, were investigated and attributed primarily to malnutrition. Scientists have pointed to chronically stressed animals living in warming oceans. Available prey has become less reliable. Coastal real estate development has added stress, limiting some of the territory they prefer for their colonies. Harmful algal blooms or red tides happen more often and are larger, affecting seal behavior and cognition. The aggressive encounters that alarmed beachgoers from 2021 onwards were initially attributed to these blooms. Researchers also point to another detail that may point to where the disease is heading: When the seal attacked Debbie Hendrikz on Fish Hoek beach, she did not contract rabies, unlike when a diseased dog bites a person. The NICD notes that to date, there are no known cases where seals transmitted the disease to people. Oelofse, who has tracked the toll of seal attacks on humans closely, called this the most interesting open question in the entire outbreak: Why has rabies not spread from infected seals to the humans they have bitten? His team has gone back and retrospectively contacted people known to have been bitten by confirmed rabid seals — none have developed rabies. Tour guides operating in the area around Duiker Island reported being bitten repeatedly by seals behaving strangely and were not treated for rabies. None became infected. “I think it might be related to the high salt content in the seal’s mouth,” Oelofse said. “It might be diluting the virus. We know salt water has a bit of an antiseptic effect. I don’t know.” Kotze cautioned against speculating on this question, “There is no proof as to why those bites would not have infected the human.” The leading theories involve reduced viral load in the saliva of marine-exposed animals, salt water degrading the virus, and the immediate wound-washing that ocean immersion provides. These theories remain unproven, he said. For now, government officials are cautious. The NICD strongly advises anyone bitten, scratched or licked by a seal suspected of having rabies to wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water and seek immediate treatment at the nearest clinic or hospital. Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis is effective in preventing infection if applied urgently and appropriately. The NICD further advises that those at frequent or continual risk of exposure, such as swimmers, divers, surfers or people working with seals, should discuss pre-exposure prophylaxis with their healthcare provider. The government has considered other efforts to limit the spread of the disease in seals. Mass vaccination of the entire seal population — an approach that has helped control rabies in European foxes — was assessed and declared not feasible by the National Department of Agriculture in its October 2024 report. A key factor cited for the decision is that seal colonies are often inaccessible. But the July 2025 workshop produced a more targeted recommendation: Vaccination trials should begin for seals that frequently interact with humans. The effectiveness of rabies vaccines in marine mammals remains unproven, but experts concluded that the trials pose minimal risk and may prove to provide protection. In August 2024, the world’s first ever rabies vaccination trial in marine mammals took place at Kalk Bay harbor in Cape Town, conducted by the Two Oceans Aquarium Foundation in collaboration with scientific and government partners. The city has since stepped back from continuing to vaccinate the Kalk Bay harbor seal colony. The high turnover of individual seals moving between that colony and Seal Island, approximately 12 km (7.6 mi) east, makes sustained coverage difficult to achieve. A renewed, smaller effort at Gordon’s Bay harbor is being considered, Oelofse said. Authorities have started and continue to vaccinate Southern elephant seals (Mirounga leonina) on the Cape coast. Even though they are a different species and the virus has not been identified in them, officials fear they may contract the disease from fights with Cape fur seals. The concern driving this effort is that elephant seals can travel far: One tagged elephant seal vaccinated in Cape Town later turned up on Marion Island, deep in the Southern Ocean, demonstrating how far and fast the disease could travel if it took hold in a more mobile, far-ranging species. Between 15 and 20 elephant seals have been tagged and vaccinated to date, with booster shots given when possible. news.content: 24/7 LivePhiladelphiaPennsylvaniaNew JerseyDelaware 81° Rabies Coyote put down in Cheltenham Twp. tested positive for rabies, police say By6abc Digital Staff Wednesday, August 26, 2026 5:04PM Watch the 6abc Philadelphia 24/7 stream featuring Action News, AccuWeather and Entertainment CHELTENHAM TWP., Pa. (WPVI) -- Police in Cheltenham Township are warning residents after a rabid coyote was killed. The coyote, which was "recently put down by police," tested positive for rabies, the police department posted on social media on Wednesday. Last week, police said they recieved multiple reports about an aggressive coyote in the Wyncote section of the Township, near Curtis Park, Hopeland Rd., Washington Lane and Rock Creek Drive. Officers tried searching the area, including using drones, but were unable to find the animal. Then, police said they got another report of the coyote attacking a resident and a dog at the Curtis Dog Park. Top Stories 'I am an innocent man': Jerry Sandusky speaks from prison ahead of court hearing | EXCLUSIVE Man hospitalized after being shot twice in Philadelphia's Parkside Neighborhood Man shot multiple times in Tioga-Nicetown section of Philadelphia When police arrived, officers were able to kill the animal, which was sent to the Pennsylvania Game Commission for rabies testing. If you or your pet had recent contact with any coyote, officials say you should seek medical or veterinary care immediately. Officials say rabies can be transmitted through contact with an infected animal's saliva, including through bites or scratches. Pets that are not current on rabies vaccinations are especially at risk, officials added. Local officials are working with the Pennsylvania Game Commission on monitoring the area. If you suspect human exposure, contact your primary care physician immediately or if you want more information contact the PA Department of Health at 877-PA-HEALTH (877-724-3258). Residents are also asked to alert police if you see any wildlife acting erratically. Report a correction or typo Copyright © 2026 WPVI-TV. All Rights Reserved. news.content_zh: 2026 年 8 月 26 日星期三,宾夕法尼亚州切尔滕纳姆镇警方在一只被杀死的土狼检测出 狂犬病 呈阳性后向居民发出警告。这只动物是在该镇的温科特地区发现的,靠近柯蒂斯公园、霍普兰路、华盛顿巷和罗克溪大道。警方此前曾收到多起该地区有攻击性郊狼的报告,并试图使用无人机定位它,但没有成功。又有报道称,这只土狼在柯蒂斯狗狗公园袭击了一名居民和一只狗,随后被杀死。官员们强调,狂犬病 可以通过接触受感染动物的唾液传播,包括咬伤或抓伤,并敦促最近接触过土狼的任何人或其宠物立即寻求医疗或兽医护理。未及时更新 狂犬病 疫苗接种 的宠物尤其面临风险。地方当局正在与宾夕法尼亚州游戏委员会合作监测该地区,并鼓励居民报告任何异常行为的野生动物。

Officials said the finding marks the first rabies case in an animal reported in the county this year. They have yet to disclose where in the region the bat was located. Rabies is a deadly virus that spreads to people from the saliva of infected animals, according to the Mayo Clinic. It's usually transmitted through a bite from a bat, coyote, fox, raccoon or skunk. Livingston County health officials say bat bites can be very small and people may be exposed to rabies even if they don't see a bite or scratch. According to health officials, exposure to rabies can also happen when a person touches a bat's saliva or brain tissue or wakes up with one in their bedroom. Children, people with developmental disabilities and intoxicated individuals may also be considered exposed if they are in a room with a bat. Anyone in Livingston County who believes they've been exposed is asked to capture the bat, report the exposure by filling out a form on the health department's website and call department staff at 517‐552‐6882 for testing guidance and next steps. Health officials say people can prevent rabies by keeping bats out of homes, vaccinating their pets and washing bites or scratches with soap and water before seeking medical help. The Michigan Department of Natural Resources says the state is home to nine species of bats. (WTOC) - A bat found on Hilton Head Island has tested positive for rabies, marking the second confirmed case of the virus in Beaufort County this year, state health officials announced. The South Carolina Department of Public Health (DPH) confirmed the positive test on Aug. 25 after the bat was found near Headlands Drive and Oyster Rake Lane. Officials said at least one person was exposed and has been referred to a healthcare provider. “Rabid bats have been known to transmit the rabies virus,” said Terri McCollister, Rabies Program manager. “People don’t always realize they or a pet have been bitten since bat teeth are tiny and bites are easy to overlook.” Health officials warning residents never to handle bats or wild animals with bare hands. If you or your pets had contact with this bat or another potentially rabid animal, call the DPH Charleston office at (843) 953-4713 during business hours, or (888) 847-0902 after hours. DPH also confirmed rabies cases this week in a Greenville County skunk, as well as bats in Greenwood and Pickens counties, bringing the statewide total to 78 cases in 2026. Copyright 2026 WTOC. Sports Scoreboard High School Sports Atlanta Braves Savannah Bananas Savannah State Georgia Southern End Zone Golf Community Birthday Club Calendar Live Healthy Morning Break Pet Pics Top Teacher The Big Give Back Senior Salutes WTOC Toy Drive Morning Break Things to Do Food Arts and Entertainment Health Music Style DIY Sponsored About Us Contact Us Download Our Apps Internships Meet The Team Antenna Tips Advertising Programming InvestigateTV PowerNation Aging Untold Local News Live NextGen TV Contests Digital Marketing Gray AI Policy Hilton Head bat tests positive for rabies; one person exposed Close By WTOC Staff Published: Aug. 27, 2026 at 4:44 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google HILTON HEAD, S.C. (WTOC) - A bat found on Hilton Head Island has tested positive for rabies, marking the second confirmed case of the virus in Beaufort County this year, state health officials announced. The South Carolina Department of Public Health (DPH) confirmed the positive test on Aug. 25 after the bat was found near Headlands Drive and Oyster Rake Lane. Officials said at least one person was exposed and has been referred to a healthcare provider. “Rabid bats have been known to transmit the rabies virus,” said Terri McCollister, Rabies Program manager. “People don’t always realize they or a pet have been bitten since bat teeth are tiny and bites are easy to overlook.” Health officials warning residents never to handle bats or wild animals with bare hands. If you or your pets had contact with this bat or another potentially rabid animal, call the DPH Charleston office at (843) 953-4713 during business hours, or (888) 847-0902 after hours. DPH also confirmed rabies cases this week in a Greenville County skunk, as well as bats in Greenwood and Pickens counties, bringing the statewide total to 78 cases in 2026. Copyright 2026 WTOC.
